# Part 1: Reproducible report and data description

## 1.1 Introduction

This report uses **Option C, the watershed conditions dataset** (`data/watershed.csv`).
The response variable is `streamflow_index`, and the three predictors are
`snowpack_pct_normal`, `precip_mm` and `mean_temp_c`. The goal is to fit and diagnose a
linear model using NumPy matrix computation: standardizing the predictors, building the
design matrix, fitting by least squares, and checking the fit with QR, SVD and condition
numbers. The data are synthetic, so no causal claims are made.

# Part 2: Matrix setup and standardization

```{python}
predictor_cols = ["snowpack_pct_normal", "precip_mm", "mean_temp_c"]
response_col = "streamflow_index"

predictors = df[predictor_cols].to_numpy()
y = df[response_col].to_numpy()
```

## Standardize the predictors

```{python}
means = predictors.mean(axis=0)
sds = predictors.std(axis=0)

Z = (predictors - means) / sds

print("Column means of Z:", np.round(Z.mean(axis=0), 10))
print("Column SDs of Z:  ", np.round(Z.std(axis=0), 10))
```

## Construct the design matrix

```{python}
X = np.column_stack([
    np.ones(len(Z)),
    Z
])

shapes = pd.DataFrame({
    "object": ["predictors", "Z", "X", "y"],
    "shape": [predictors.shape, Z.shape, X.shape, y.shape],
})
shapes
```

```{python}
print("Matrix rank of X:", np.linalg.matrix_rank(X))
print("Number of predictors (excluding intercept):", X.shape[1] - 1)
```

**Written response.** For least squares, `X` must have one row per observation, so its
number of rows has to match the length of `y`. Otherwise there is no fitted value to pair
with each response, and `X @ beta_hat` cannot be compared with `y`. The column of ones is
the intercept, which lets the fitted plane sit at the mean level of the response instead of
being forced through the origin. Standardizing put every predictor on the same scale, with
mean 0 and standard deviation 1, so the coefficients are comparable and the intercept
equals the mean of the response. Broadcasting makes this possible without a loop: the
length-3 vectors `means` and `sds` are automatically stretched across all rows of the
(n × 3) `predictors` array, so each column is centered and scaled by its own mean and SD.

# Part 3: Least squares

```{python}
beta_hat, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(
    X,
    y,
    rcond=None
)

coef_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "term": ["intercept"] + predictor_cols,
    "estimate": beta_hat,
})
coef_table
```

```{python}
slopes = coef_table.iloc[1:]
largest = slopes.loc[slopes["estimate"].abs().idxmax()]

print(f"Intercept: {beta_hat[0]:.4f}")
for name, b in zip(predictor_cols, beta_hat[1:]):
    print(f"Coefficient for standardized {name}: {b:.4f}")
print(f"Largest coefficient in absolute value: {largest['term']} ({largest['estimate']:.4f})")
print(f"Mean of y (should equal the intercept): {y.mean():.4f}")
```

```{python}
fitted = X @ beta_hat
residuals = y - fitted

rmse = np.sqrt(
    np.mean(
        residuals ** 2
    )
)

print(f"Residual mean: {residuals.mean():.3e}")
print(f"RMSE: {rmse:.4f}")
```

Because the predictors are standardized, each slope is the expected change in
`streamflow_index` for a one-standard-deviation increase in that predictor, holding the
other two fixed. The intercept is the predicted streamflow index at the average value of
all three predictors. The largest standardized coefficient is identified in the output
above.

**Written response.** `X @ beta_hat` is the matrix-vector product that gives the fitted
value for each observation: the intercept plus each standardized predictor times its
coefficient. When an intercept column is present, the least squares normal equations force
the residuals to be orthogonal to the column of ones, which means they sum to zero, so the
residual mean is zero up to floating-point rounding. RMSE summarizes the typical size of a
prediction error in the units of the response. `X * beta_hat` is elementwise
multiplication: broadcasting multiplies each column of `X` by its coefficient and returns an
(n × 4) matrix, while `X @ beta_hat` also sums across each row and returns the length-n
vector of fitted values.

# Part 4: QR, SVD, and conditioning

## QR decomposition

```{python}
Q, R = np.linalg.qr(X)

print("Shape of Q:", Q.shape)
print("Shape of R:", R.shape)
print("Q @ R ≈ X:", np.allclose(Q @ R, X))
print("Q.T @ Q ≈ I:", np.allclose(Q.T @ Q, np.eye(Q.shape[1])))
```

## SVD

```{python}
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(
    X,
    full_matrices=False
)

print("Shape of U: ", U.shape)
print("Shape of s: ", s.shape)
print("Shape of Vt:", Vt.shape)
print("Singular values:", np.round(s, 4))
```

```{python}
X_reconstructed = (
    U
    @ np.diag(s)
    @ Vt
)

print("U @ diag(s) @ Vt ≈ X:", np.allclose(X_reconstructed, X))
```

## Rank and conditioning

```{python}
X_raw = np.column_stack([
    np.ones(len(predictors)),
    predictors
])

rank_X = np.linalg.matrix_rank(X)
cond_X = np.linalg.cond(X)
cond_X_raw = np.linalg.cond(X_raw)

print(f"Rank of X: {rank_X}")
print(f"Condition number of standardized X: {cond_X:.4f}")
print(f"Condition number of raw X_raw: {cond_X_raw:.4f}")
print(f"Ratio raw / standardized: {cond_X_raw / cond_X:.1f}")
```

```{python}
# Correlations among predictors, to help interpret the singular values
pd.DataFrame(
    np.corrcoef(Z, rowvar=False),
    index=predictor_cols,
    columns=predictor_cols,
).round(3)
```

**Written response.** `Q @ R ≈ X` verifies that the QR factorization is correct: the
orthonormal basis `Q` combined with the upper-triangular `R` rebuilds the design matrix.
`Q.T @ Q ≈ I` verifies that the columns of `Q` are orthonormal, with unit length and
mutually perpendicular. The singular values measure how much `X` stretches vectors along
its principal directions: large singular values mark directions the data span strongly, and
the smallest one marks the weakest direction. Here the smallest singular value reflects the
correlation between snowpack and precipitation, shown in the correlation table. A large
condition number, the ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value, would mean
that small changes in the data could produce large changes in the coefficients, which is a
sign of near-collinearity or poor scaling. Standardization reduced the condition number
dramatically, as the output above shows. The raw condition number is large because the
columns are on very different scales (a column of ones, precipitation in the hundreds of
millimetres, and temperature around ten degrees), so the matrix is badly scaled even
though the underlying relationships are the same. The standardized condition number is
small, so the standardized design shows no evidence of severe near-redundancy among the
predictors, although the moderate correlation between snowpack and precipitation makes
one direction weaker than the others.

# Part 5: Reproducibility and numerical-computing reflection

Clean execution matters because a computational report is only trustworthy if someone else
can run it and get the same results. If the report renders from top to bottom in a fresh
session, every table and number is a direct consequence of the code and the data, rather
than of steps I happened to run interactively. This is why reusable code should not depend
on hidden notebook state. In a notebook, it is easy to run cells out of order, delete a cell
that defined a variable, or overwrite an object, and the notebook will still appear to work
until it is restarted. Code that depends on that state breaks for anyone else, including me
a week later.

For fitting the model, `np.linalg.lstsq()` is preferable to computing (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy by hand.
Forming XᵀX squares the condition number of X, so any near-collinearity or poor scaling is
magnified, and explicitly inverting a matrix is both slower and less accurate than solving
the system directly. `lstsq` uses an SVD-based solver that is numerically stable and also
handles rank-deficient designs gracefully.

Checks such as `np.allclose()` are preferable to exact equality because floating-point
arithmetic introduces tiny rounding errors. A QR or SVD reconstruction will match X only up
to differences on the order of 10⁻¹⁵, so testing with `==` would report failure even when the
decomposition is correct. A tolerance-based comparison asks the right question: are these
equal to within numerical precision?

The condition-number comparison showed me that a diagnostic can be driven by measurement
scale rather than by the substance of the data. The raw design matrix looked badly
conditioned only because its columns were on very different scales; after standardization,
the condition number was small, and the only remaining structure was the modest correlation
between snowpack and precipitation. So a large condition number should prompt me to check
the scaling before concluding that predictors are redundant.

The practice I will carry into the final project is rendering the report from the
repository root with relative paths, then restarting and re-running everything before each
commit, so that the version on GitHub always reproduces the results I report.
